clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Aortic Stenosis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Aortic Stenosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes avoidance of hypotension; use nitrates or other vasodilators only cautiously with monitoring when clinically necessary in severe AS, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fainted while walking up a hill and chest tightness on exertion

Key HPI features: Presents with a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath when climbing stairs or walking uphill. Yesterday, while carrying groceries up a steep street, experienced tight retrosternal chest discomfort and suddenly lost consciousness for approximately 30 seconds (exertional syncope). Recovered spontaneously with no post-ictal confusion or tongue biting. Denies palpitations or symptoms at rest.

Objective/Exam findings: Check vitals (narrow pulse pressure e.g., 110/85 mmHg). Cardiac auscultation: harsh, crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotid arteries. Slow-rising, sustained carotid pulse ('pulsus parvus et tardus') and sustained apex beat. ECG (left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern). Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE).
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension x15 years, hypercholesterolaemia, mild osteoarthritis of knees
Current medications: ramipril 10mg OD, amlodipine 5mg OD, atorvastatin 40mg ON
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Aortic Stenosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope on exertion — a marker of severe stenosis and sudden-death risk.
management_principles: Avoid hypotension; use nitrates or other vasodilators only cautiously with monitoring when clinically necessary in severe AS
Urgent cardiology referral for urgent transthoracic echocardiogram to quantify aortic valve area and mean gradient
Workup for Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR) vs Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 75M with HTN presents with exertional syncope, exertional angina, and progressive dyspnoea over 6 months. No post-ictal features. Spontaneous recovery.
reference_soap.objective: Check vitals (narrow pulse pressure e.g., 110/85 mmHg). Cardiac auscultation: harsh, crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotid arteries. Slow-rising, sustained carotid pulse ('pulsus parvus et tardus') and sustained apex beat. ECG (left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern). Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE).
reference_soap.assessment: Severe calcific aortic valve stenosis with cardinal triad symptoms (syncope, angina, dyspnoea). DDx: vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension from antihypertensives, cardiac arrhythmia (complete heart block/VT), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
reference_soap.plan: Avoid hypotension; use nitrates or other vasodilators only cautiously with monitoring when clinically necessary in severe AS. Urgent cardiology referral for urgent transthoracic echocardiogram to quantify aortic valve area and mean gradient. Workup for Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR) vs Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI). Advise to avoid strenuous exertion until evaluated.

learning_objectives: Elicit the classical symptom triad of severe aortic stenosis: exertional dyspnoea, exertional angina, and exertional syncope
Identify classical physical signs: slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, and ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids
Explain the hemodynamic contraindication of aggressive vasodilators/nitrates in fixed left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Outline the comparative indications for Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement vs Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in elderly patients

teaching.one_liner: A calcified valve throttles blood leaving the heart. Syncope, angina and breathlessness on exertion are its cardinal triad.
red_flags: Syncope on exertion — a marker of severe stenosis and sudden-death risk

must_ask.objective: Syncope and its relation to exertion
must_ask.say: Did you faint while you were exerting yourself, or at rest?
Do you get chest tightness when you walk up a hill?
How far can you walk on the flat before you have to stop for breath?
Has this been getting worse over months, or did it come on suddenly?
Has a doctor ever told you that you have a heart murmur?
What are you most worried this might be?
